note: Written by the reviewing agent. decision_check.py checks every step against the real code and attaches the real evidence results.

decisions.title: The analyzer stops crashing on bad keys

steps.text: a repeated key was added a second time with `intMembers.Add`, and that crashed.
after the mixed-key warning (`DoNotMixStringAndIntKeys`), the code went on with the bad member.
a key is stored only if it is not there yet (`!intMembers.ContainsKey`).
a member with the wrong kind of key is skipped (`continue`) after its warning.
the fields loop gets the same guard (`!stringMembers.ContainsKey`).

decisions.verdict: We accept this: bad keys now give the user a warning instead of a crash.

because.text: Four new tests crash on the old code and pass on the new code.
We ran the real analyzer on small examples. The second member of a repeated key now gets the warning.

decisions.title: Normal keys can no longer crash it

steps.text: a member's key is a different kind from the first one (`isIntKey && intKey == null`),
it is skipped (`continue`).
a number key is already taken (`!intMembers.ContainsKey(member.IntKey)`), the member is not stored again.
text keys follow the same rule (`!stringMembers.ContainsKey(member.StringKey)`).
the fields loop never adds a key twice either (`intMembers.Add`).

decisions.verdict: We accept this: for number and text keys, a proof and many real runs show the code no longer crashes.

because.text: A proof tool shows a model of this code never fails for number and text keys. The model gives the same answer as the real code on every input we tried.

decisions.unsure: The proof is about a model. We compared it with the real code only for types with up to 4 members.

decisions.title: An empty key still crashes it

steps.text: the first field has an empty key, so `isIntKey = intKey != null` treats the type as using text keys.
the fields loop uses a bare `else`, so it goes on with no key at all.
`stringMembers.ContainsKey(stringKey!)` gets nothing and crashes.
the new guard (`!stringMembers.ContainsKey(member.StringKey)`) comes too late to help.
the properties loop checks `else if (stringKey is not null)`, so it does not crash.

decisions.verdict: We flag the fix as incomplete: a field with an empty key still crashes the analyzer, even for opted-out types.

because.text: We ran the real analyzer on this case. It crashes before and after the change.
The proof tool found the same case on its own. It is the only way the new code still fails.

decisions.title: One warning is now lost

steps.text: after the mixed-key warning (`DoNotMixStringAndIntKeys`), the code went on.
so it also checked the member's own type (`this.CollectCore(item.Type, item)`), which can give a second warning.
it stops at `continue`, right after the first warning.
the check of the member's type (`this.CollectCore(item.Type, item)`) never runs for that member.
the fields loop has the same `continue`.

decisions.verdict: We will not accept this on our own: a warning users got before now disappears, so the analyzer's owner must decide.

because.text: We ran the real analyzer on a member with a mixed key and a type that cannot be saved. The old code warned about the type. The new code does not.

decisions.unsure: The member still gets the mixed-key warning. That may be enough, but it is a product choice.
decisions.ask: Is it fine to lose the type warning when the member's key is already wrong?

impact.who: Users whose type mixes string and int keys and also has a member whose type cannot be saved.
impact.effect: Their build still fails, on the mixed-key error. Only after they fix the keys does the type error show up. They lose one fix-and-rebuild round; nothing broken can ship.

decisions.title: First member wins, repeats get warned

steps.text: a number key is already used (`intMembers.ContainsKey(intKey!.Value)`), a 'keys must be unique' warning is shown (`KeysMustBeUnique`).
the member is stored only if its key is new (`!intMembers.ContainsKey`), so the first one stays.
text keys work the same way (`!stringMembers.ContainsKey`).
the fields loop does the same (`!intMembers.ContainsKey(member.IntKey)`).

decisions.verdict: We accept this: every repeated key gets a warning, and the first member is the one kept.

because.text: The repeated-key tests crash on the old code and pass on the new code.
The proof tool shows the first member wins and every repeat is warned. Its model matches the real code.
Our experiment on the real analyzer shows the second member gets the warning.

decisions.title: The same fix is written twice

steps.text: the properties loop gets a new guard (`if (!intMembers.ContainsKey(member.IntKey))`).
the fields loop gets the very same lines (`if (!intMembers.ContainsKey(member.IntKey))`).
both loops get the same `continue`.
text keys are also copied in both places (`if (!stringMembers.ContainsKey(member.StringKey))`).

decisions.verdict: We note this as a cost, not a bug: both copies must be kept in step by hand.

because.text: A script counted copied code in this file before and after the change. It grew.

decisions.title: Half the new tests pass anyway

steps.text: `MemberWithoutKeyIsReported` checks a member with no key.
`AllowPrivateRequiredIsReported` checks a private member.
`MemberTypeMustBeMessagePackObjectIsReported` checks the member's type.
`SourceGenerationOnlyDiagnosticsAreNotReportedWhenSuppressed` checks warnings that should stay quiet.

decisions.verdict: We count these four as guards for old behaviour, not as proof the fix works.

because.text: We ran each new test on the old and the new code. These four pass on both.

decisions.title: Run-time tests pass, before and after

steps.text: a type `SuppressedSourceGenerationType` opts out with `SuppressSourceGeneration = true`.
one test expects no generated code for it (`Assert.Null`).
another saves and loads it (`MessagePackSerializer.Serialize`) and checks the values come back.

decisions.verdict: We accept this: both tests pass. They pass on the old code too, so they guard the behaviour; they do not prove the fix.

because.text: With SDK 9 the test project builds. The pinned SDK 8.0.402 could not load the code generator.
Both tests pass before and after the change.

decisions.unsure: The repo pins SDK 8.0.402. We ran with 9.0.321 because that SDK could not load the generator.

decisions.title: The new help text promises too much

steps.text: the README says the analyzer still checks opted-out types (`The analyzer still validates these types`).
it promises keys are unique and of one kind (`Keys are unique and all of the same kind`).
it promises a check that types can be reached (`MsgPack012`).
it says some checks are skipped for these types (`MsgPack011`).

decisions.verdict: We do not trust this text yet: one promise has no test, and the key check can still crash.

because.text: Our experiment shows the key check still crashes on a field with an empty key.
The new tests cover most promises, but none checks that types can be reached.

decisions.title: Type warning skipped after key warning

steps.text: a member has the wrong kind of key, the code now stops at `continue`.
it never checks the member's type (`this.CollectCore(item.Type, item)`).
the fields loop does the same (`continue`).

decisions.verdict: We report this: a member with a mixed key no longer gets the warning about its type.

because.text: Our experiment on the real analyzer confirms the type check is skipped.

decisions.title: An empty key in a field crashes

steps.text: the properties loop checks `else if (stringKey is not null)`.
the fields loop uses a bare `else`.
with an empty key, `stringMembers.ContainsKey(stringKey!)` gets nothing and crashes.

decisions.verdict: We report the fix as incomplete: one simple case still crashes the analyzer.

because.text: Our experiment shows the crash before and after the change.
The proof tool points at the same case.

decisions.title: Our own goal was too strong

steps.text: the first member decides the key kind (`isIntKey = intKey != null`).
that member is a field with an empty key, the bare `else` still runs,
`stringMembers.ContainsKey(stringKey!)` fails.

decisions.verdict: We dropped the goal 'it never fails' and kept the exact rule the proof found instead.

because.text: The proof tool shows 'never fails' is false, and names the one case where it fails.

decisions.title: A suspected problem was fine

steps.text: a text key is already used (`stringMembers.ContainsKey(stringKey!)`), the 'must be unique' warning is shown (`KeysMustBeUnique`).
the first member stays, because a new key is stored only once (`!stringMembers.ContainsKey(member.StringKey)`).

decisions.verdict: We dropped this worry: the second member of a repeated key does get the warning.

because.text: Our experiment on the real analyzer shows the second member is warned.

decisions.title: The crash was not about opting out

steps.text: any type with a repeated key crashed at `intMembers.Add`, opted out or not.
the test `DuplicateKeysAreReportedWithoutAnalyzerFailureForGeneratedTypes` uses a normal type (`[MessagePackObject]`).
it expects only the warning (`MsgPack005`), and it fails on the old code.

decisions.verdict: We note that the fix helps all types, not just opted-out ones, and that opted-out types were already checked before.

because.text: We ran the new tests on the old code. Some pass there, some crash.

decisions.title: Test file name breaks a style rule

steps.text: the first type in the file is `SuppressedSourceGenerationType`.
the file is named after the second type, `SuppressedSourceGenerationTests`.

decisions.verdict: We report a small style problem: the file name should match its first type.

because.text: The build log for that project shows this style warning.

decisions.title: An old warning shows blanks

steps.text: the properties loop fills in the type and member names (`item.Name`) for `BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull`.
the fields loop sends `BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull` with only a place, and no names.
the user sees '{0}.{1}' instead of names. This line was not changed (`Diagnostic.Create`).

decisions.verdict: We note an older bug outside this change: the field warning text has blanks.

decisions.title: Extra help text was added

steps.text: the README gets a new section, `Opting out of source generation`.
it lists which checks still run (`The analyzer still validates these types`).

decisions.verdict: We flag this as beyond the issue, which asked only for an analyzer fix. It is harmless but needs its own review.

because.text: A script flagged one change that touches user help text.

decisions.title: The fix is made twice, in two copied loops

steps.text: before the fix, the fields loop already repeated the properties loop line for line (`intMembers.Add(member.IntKey, (member, item.Type));`).
the properties loop gets a skip (`continue`) and a guard before `intMembers.Add`.
the fields loop gets the same edits (`continue`, `stringMembers.Add`).

decisions.verdict: We flag this as a maintenance cost, not a bug: the fix is typed into two loops that were already copies, so the next fix there must also be made twice.

because.text: The tool counts copied lines in this file: 244 before, 258 after. 6 of the 10 added code lines sit in copied blocks.
Copied blocks in this file went from 10 to 12.

decisions.unsure: One shared helper for both loops would remove the copy, but it touches code the issue did not ask about. Rule H-20 favours the fuller fix; the owner decides.

decisions.title: The same skip, added in both loops

steps.text: a property's key kind does not match the others, the properties loop now stops at `continue`.
the fields loop gets the identical line (`continue`).

decisions.verdict: Two copies of one decision. If someone later changes one and not the other, properties and fields will treat a mixed key differently.

because.text: The tool found this added line twice in the same file.

decisions.title: The number-key guard, added in both loops

steps.text: a repeated number key is already reported a few lines up (`KeysMustBeUnique`).
the properties loop adds the member only if its number is new (`if (!intMembers.ContainsKey(member.IntKey))`).
the fields loop adds the same two lines (`intMembers.Add(member.IntKey, (member, item.Type));`).

decisions.verdict: The guard is right, but it now lives in two places. A later change to how repeated keys are handled must find both.

because.text: The tool found this added two-line block twice in the same file.

decisions.title: The name-key guard, added in both loops

steps.text: the properties loop adds the member only if its name key is new (`if (!stringMembers.ContainsKey(member.StringKey))`).
the fields loop adds the same two lines (`stringMembers.Add(member.StringKey, (member, item.Type));`).

decisions.verdict: Same as the number-key guard: correct, but kept in two places that must change together.

because.text: The tool found this added two-line block twice in the same file.
